extracted.intended_audience: U.S. Patent Examiners (and patent practitioners evaluating or prosecuting design patents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining design patent applications, including how to reject or evaluate claims under 35 U.S.C. 171 (ornamentality), 35 U.S.C. 102 (novelty), and 35 U.S.C. 103 (nonobviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner prima facie burden for non-ornamentality rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: To properly reject a claimed design under 35 U.S.C. 171 on the basis of a lack of ornamentality, an examiner must make a prima facie showing that the claimed design lacks ornamentality and provide a sufficient evidentiary basis for factual assumptions relied upon in such showing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Oetiker; examiner bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of unpatentability; when evidence is common knowledge the examiner should take official notice (see MPEP § 2144.03). Rejections should not be made in absence of such evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of evidence establishing lack of ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of proper evidentiary basis for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 that a claim is lacking in ornamentality would be common knowledge in the art, the appearance of the design itself, the specification of a related utility patent, information provided in the specification, or the fact that an article would be hidden during its ultimate end use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence is based on common knowledge or 'well-known' facts, take official notice and state it; insert source of evidence (utility patent, brochure, response to letter of inquiry, etc.) in examiner notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two categories of lack-of-ornamentality rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejections under 35 U.S.C. 171 as lacking in ornamentality based on a proper prima facie showing fall into two categories: (A) a design visible in its ultimate end use which is primarily functional based on the evidence of record; or (B) a design not visible in its ultimate hidden end use which is itself evidence that the design is primarily functional, unless the design 'is clearly intended to be noticed during the process of sale.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite appropriate case law (e.g., In re Stevens; In re Webb) and evaluate visibility and intent to be noticed during sale when applying category (B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shift to applicant after prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: When the examiner has established a proper prima facie case of lack of ornamentality, 'the burden of coming forward with evidence or argument shifts to the applicant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may overcome rejection by providing evidence (e.g., affidavits/declarations) showing intent to create design for the 'purpose of ornamenting' (In re Carletti).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable evidence to establish ornamentality (affidavits/declarations)
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 may be submitted over applicant’s signature explaining, specifically and in depth, which features or areas of the claimed design were created with 'thought of ornament.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavit must be specific and in-depth. Declarations from representatives of the company which commissioned the design are also acceptable if they explain which features were created with ornament in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative designs and advertisements as evidence of ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Within affidavits/declarations, possible alternative ornamental designs which could have served the same function may be submitted as evidence that the appearance was the result of ornamental considerations. Advertisements emphasizing the ornamentality of the article may also be submitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite L. A. Gear v. Thom McAn and Berry Sterling Corp. v. Pescor Plastics as supportive authorities; include clear examples to show choice driven by ornament, not function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hidden-designs: need to show period of visibility ('matter of concern')
rubrics_metrics.description: For articles hidden during end use, applicant must establish that there was a period between manufacture/assembly and ultimate use when the article's appearance was a 'matter of concern' to prospective customers, and that during this period the design as a whole was created for the 'purpose of ornamenting' or with 'thought of ornament.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant can submit customer affidavits attesting to concern with design, commercial practices showing visibility, or other evidence demonstrating that ornamentality was a consideration during that period (cites In re Webb, Larson v. Classic Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Attorney argument insufficient to establish ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: Attorney arguments are insufficient to establish such intent as only the applicant can know the motivation behind the creation of a design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on applicant's or commissioning company's signed declaration/affidavit rather than counsel statements (Power Controls Corp. v. Hybrinetics; Ex parte Webb).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade shows/catalog inclusion generally insufficient to establish ornamentality
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere display of the article embodying the design at trade shows or its inclusion in catalogs is insufficient to establish ornamentality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be clear and specific indication of ornamentality in such evidence for it to have probative weight (Ex parte Webb; Berry Sterling v. Pescor Plastics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner evaluation of ornamentality evidence — design as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must evaluate evidence in light of the design as a whole to decide if the claim is primarily ornamental; determination is not based on the size or amount of features identified as ornamental but rather on their influence on the overall appearance of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess influence on overall appearance rather than counting features or measuring size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and ornamentality requirements to overcome hidden-design rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirements of visibility and ornamentality must be met for a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 171 based on the article being hidden during its end use to be overcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere possibilities (e.g., encasing a concealed element in a transparent cover) are insufficient; applicant must provide factual evidence of visibility and ornamentality during the relevant period (Norco Products v. Mecca Development).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simulation/originality requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 171 requires that a design be 'original.' A design which simulates an existing object or person is not original and should be rejected as lacking originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rejecting on simulation grounds, provide evidence of the appearance of the object/person being simulated so a comparison can be made; consider concurrent rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102 or 103(a) if prior art anticipates or renders obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form of simulation rejection and explanatory evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting simulation (entire article), include the name/source of the article or person being simulated and, where appropriate, follow with a paragraph explaining the evidence cited (e.g., applicant’s design has in no way departed from the natural appearance of [simulated object]).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Insert source identifiers in examiner notes and use form paragraphs (¶ 15.08.02, ¶ 15.08.03) to explain evidence and comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive subject matter rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Design applications disclosing subject matter that could be deemed offensive to any race, religion, sex, ethnic group, or nationality (e.g., caricatures or depictions) should be rejected as nonstatutory subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 171.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such material also implicates 37 CFR 1.3 (decorum and courtesy); use Form Paragraph 15.10 and see MPEP § 608.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty standard for design patents (average observer test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard for determining novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102 is that 'the degree of difference [from the prior art] required to establish novelty occurs when the average observer takes the new design for a different, and not a modified, already-existing design.' The reference must show the same subject matter and be identical in all material respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Bartlett and Hupp v. Siroflex; the average observer is not charged with knowledge of the art—analogousness of prior art need not be raised for 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/hidden features not counted for novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102, features of the design which are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differences solely in functional considerations do not negate anticipation; if applicant wants to rely on such features, they must first establish ornamentality under 35 U.S.C. 171 (see MPEP § 1504.01(c)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign filing/priority and 102(d)/172 practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Registration of a design abroad is considered equivalent to patenting under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) and 35 U.S.C. 102(d). The U.S. design application must be made within 6 months of the foreign filing to claim priority for designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections under 102(d)/172 should only be made when the examiner knows the foreign registration/patent actually issued before the U.S. filing date based on an application filed more than six months prior; include form paragraph ¶ 15.03.01 when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs for 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs are provided for rejections under the various subsections of 35 U.S.C. 102 (¶ 15.11 through ¶ 15.17) to state the statutory basis for anticipation or statutory bars (102(a)–(g)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate form paragraph and insert the cited reference or basis in the bracketed fields as instructed in examiner notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design patents concern ornamental appearance only
rubrics_metrics.description: Design patent applications are concerned solely with the ornamental appearance of an article of manufacture; functional and/or structural features are not considered in design cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function and structure are matters for utility patent applications; do not permit functional/structural features to substitute for ornamental claim elements (see ¶ 15.41).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness evaluation (Graham factors adapted for design)
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic factual inquiries for obviousness (Graham) apply to designs: (A) determining scope and content of the prior art; (B) ascertaining differences between the claimed design and the prior art; (C) resolving the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (D) evaluating secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these factors in the design context; collect facts to support prima facie obviousness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prior art for design obviousness (analogous arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of relevant prior art for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) extends to all 'analogous arts.' Whether references are analogous depends on whether the appearance of ornamental features in one would suggest their application to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the problem is merely giving an attractive appearance to a surface, analogousness is broad (wallpaper, oven door, crockery may be analogous); if differences involve shape/form, the nature of the articles matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed design — overall appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining 35 U.S.C. 103(a) patentability, it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered. Mere differences are not alone sufficient for patentability; identify all differences and state if any are de minimis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Leslie and In re Lamb; when differences are de minimis from a design viewpoint, the rejection should so state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill for design obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of ordinary skill in the art for design obviousness is that of the 'designer' of the types of articles presented; obviousness must be judged from that perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Nalbandian and In re Carter; evaluate what would be obvious to a designer of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations relevant to design obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations, such as commercial success and copying of the design by others, are relevant to the evaluation of obviousness of a design claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider evidence of nonobviousness either during prima facie evaluation or in rebuttal of an obviousness rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness standard for designs
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish prima facie obviousness, all the claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art; the proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Graham inquiries adapted for design; ensure references together teach/suggest all claim limitations to support a prima facie obviousness finding (In re Nalbandian).
